text: There have been two New Brighton Piers in the Christchurch, New Zealand, suburb of New Brighton. The first pier, constructed from timber, opened on 18 January 1894 and was demolished on 12 October 1965. Construction began in 1891, and the opening ceremony was officially conducted by the Governor of New Zealand, the Lord Glasgow, with attendees including the Mayor of Christchurch (Walter Cooper), the Mayor of Linwood (J. R. Brunt), and two members of the House of Representatives (George John Smith and William Whitehouse Collins). The event ended as it started to rain, causing the planned fireworks to be postponed. The pier was built to a length of 700 feet (210 m), with plans for an octagonal end and a large building that were never realized. Over time, the structure deteriorated, and the city council ordered its demolition, which occurred during four and a half hours in the early morning of 12 October 1965 on a receding tide. For 30 years, the New Brighton community campaigned for a new pier, with the Pier and Foreshore Society leading efforts to save the original and later advocating for a replacement. When NZ$2 million was raised, Christchurch City Council matched the funding, and a new pier was designed using reinforced concrete. This current pier was built in the exact same location and officially opened on 1 November 1997. It spans 300 metres (980 ft), making it the longest ocean pier in Australasia. The New Brighton Pier is regarded as the icon of New Brighton and later the icon of Christchurch following the 22 February 2011 earthquake that severely damaged Christchurch's Cathedral. It is one of Christchurch's major tourist attractions and currently hosts various events, including regular skate-on-the-pier activities and the annual Guy Fawkes fireworks display on 5 November. The pier sustained damage from several earthquakes, with the 2016 Christchurch earthquake worsening the damage. Repairs began in February 2017, lasted 16 months, and cost NZ$8.5 million, after which the pier reopened in May 2018. Its coordinates are 43°30′23″S 172°43′59″E or 43.5065°S 172.7330°E.
